parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the smooth cubic curve \(D\subset\mathbb{P}^2\) defined by \(x^3+y^3+z^3=0\).  Let \(L_t\) be the line given by the homogeneous equation \(x + t\,y + z = 0\).  The line \(L_t\) corresponds to a point in the dual projective plane; it is tangent to \(D\) exactly when that point lies on the dual curve \(D^{\vee}\).  Determine the real value of the parameter \(t\) for which \(L_t\) is tangent to \(D\).  Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a).  Consider a finite étale morphism \(f:X\to Y\) of degree \(N = \lceil x \rceil\) defined over \(\mathbb{Z}\).  Compute the limit as \(p\to\infty\) of the average size of the fibers \(f^{-1}(y)\) for \(y\in Y(\mathbb{F}_p)\).  Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Let y = your answer to part (b).  Using the parametrization of plane conics by symmetric \(3\times3\) matrices, consider the conic defined by the matrix
\[ M = \begin{pmatrix} y & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. \]
Compute the determinant of \(M\).  Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

points where the morphism is étale.

\boxed{100.0000}

Using the fact that the average size of the fiber f^{-1}(y) over y\in\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p) tends to the degree of f as p\to\infty, compute this limiting average. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the homogeneous binary forms in variables u,v:

    f(u,v)=u^2 - x\,v^2,\qquad g(u,v)=u - v.

Compute the resultant Res_{u}(f,g) as a polynomial in the parameter x, then evaluate this polynomial at the numeric value of x obtained from part (a). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c

Let y = your answer to part (b). Consider the family of plane curves in \mathbb{P}^2\times\mathbb{P}^1 given by the homogeneous equation

    F_t(X,Y,Z)=X^2 + Y^2 - y\,t\,Z^2,

where t is the coordinate on the base \mathbb{P}^1. By generic smoothness, the morphism to the base is smooth (hence flat) away from the points where the discriminant D(t)=t^2 - y vanishes. Determine the number of points of the base \mathbb{P}^1 (counted without multiplicity) at which the morphism fails to be flat. parts.text: Let f(x,y) = 2x^2 + 3xy + 5y^2 and g(x,y) = 7x^2 + 11xy + 13y^2 be two homogeneous binary quadratics. Compute the resultant Res_x(f,g) (i.e., eliminate the variable x) and evaluate it as a number. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the family of plane conics in \(\mathbb{P}^2 \times \mathbb{A}^1_u\) given by \[F_u(X,Y,Z)= X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 + (u^2 - x) X Z = 0.\] Using generic smoothness, determine the values of the parameter \(u\) for which the fiber is singular, and then compute the product of all such singular parameter values. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Let \(Y = \mathbb{A}^1 \setminus \{0\}\) be a connected base over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, and let \(f : X \to Y\) be the finite étale morphism obtained by adjoining a \( |y| \)-th root of the coordinate function (i.e., \(X = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_Y[t]/(t^{|y|} - u)\)). Using the transitivity of the geometric monodromy group of this cover, determine the number of geometric points in each fiber of \(f\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

For  
\[
f(x,y)=2x^{2}+3xy+5y^{2},\qquad 
g(x,y)=7x^{2}+11xy+13y^{2},
\]
write them as quadratics in \(x\):
\[
f=a_0x^{2}+a_1x+a_2,\qquad a_0=2,\;a_1=3y,\;a_2=5y^{2},
\]
\[
g=b_0x^{2}+b_1x+b_2,\qquad b_0=7,\;b_1=11y,\;b_2=13y^{2}.
\]

The resultant of two quadratics is  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_x(f,g)=a_0^{2}b_2^{2}-a_0a_1b_1b_2+a_0a_2b_1^{2}+a_1^{2}b_0b_2-a_1a_2b_0b_1+a_2^{2}b_0^{2}.
\]

Substituting the coefficients:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Res}_x(f,g) &=
4(13y^{2})^{2}-2(3y)(11y)(13y^{2})+2(5y^{2})(11y)^{2}\\
&\qquad +(3y)^{2}\,7\,(13y^{2})-(3y)(5y^{2})\,7\,(11y)+(5y^{2})^{2}\,7^{2}\\[2mm]
&=676y^{4}-858y^{4}+1210y^{4}+819y^{4}-1155y^{4}+1225y^{4}\\
&=1917\,y^{4}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Evaluating at \(y=1\) (the usual convention for a homogeneous resultant) gives the numeric value  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_x(f,g)=1917.
\]

\[
\boxed{1917.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Set \(x=1917\). The conic family is  

\[
F_u(X,Y,Z)=X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}+(u^{2}-x)XZ=0 .
\]

Its quadratic form matrix is  

\[
Q=\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & a\\[2pt]
0 & 1 & 0\\[2pt]
a & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad a=\dfrac{u^{2}-x}{2}.
\]

A conic in \(\mathbb{P}^{2}\) is singular iff \(\det Q=0\):
\[
\det Q = 1-a^{2}=0\;\Longrightarrow\; a^{2}=1.
\]

Thus \(\displaystyle \frac{u^{2}-x}{2}= \pm 1\), i.e.  

\[
u^{2}=x\pm 2.
\]

The singular parameters are  

\[
u=\pm\sqrt{x+2},\qquad u=\pm\sqrt{x-2}.
\]

Their product is  

\[
\bigl(\sqrt{x+2}\,(-\sqrt{x+2})\bigr)\,
\bigl(\sqrt{x-2}\,(-\sqrt{x-2})\bigr)
=-(x+2)\,[-(x-2)]=(x+2)(x-2)=x^{2}-4.
\]

With \(x=1917\),

\[
x^{2}-4 = 1917^{2}-4 = 3\,674\,889-4 = 3\,674\,885.
\]

\[
\boxed{3674885.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Let \(y = 3\,674\,885\).  
The morphism  

\[
f : X\longrightarrow Y,\qquad 
X=\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(\mathcal{O}_{Y}[t]/(t^{|y|}-u)\bigr),
\]

is a cyclic cover of degree \(|y| = 3\,674\,885\).  
Because the base \(Y=\mathbb{A}^{1}\setminus\{0\}\) is connected and the cover is étale, the geometric monodromy group acts transitively on each fiber. Hence every geometric fiber consists of exactly \(|y|\) points.

\[
\boxed{3674885.0000}
\]

---

\]

**Part (b)**  

Put \(x=139\).  
The conic  

\[
F_u(X,Y,Z)=X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}+(u^{2}-139)XZ
\]

has associated symmetric matrix  

\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & \dfrac{u^{2}-139}{2}\\[4pt]
0 & 1 & 0\\[4pt]
\dfrac{u^{2}-139}{2} & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its determinant is  

\[
\det A = 1-\frac{(u^{2}-139)^{2}}{4}.
\]

Singular fibres occur when \(\det A=0\):

\[
1-\frac{(u^{2}-139)^{2}}{4}=0\;\Longrightarrow\;(u^{2}-139)^{2}=4
\]
\[
\Longrightarrow\;u^{2}=139\pm2\;=\;141\ \text{or}\ 137.
\]

Hence the singular parameters are  

\[
u=\pm\sqrt{141},\qquad u=\pm\sqrt{137}.
\]

The product of all four values is  

\[
(\sqrt{141})(-\sqrt{141})(\sqrt{137})(-\sqrt{137})
= (-141)(-137)=141\cdot137=19317.
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{19317.0000}.
\]

**Part (c)**  

Here \(|y| = 19317\).  
The cover  

\[
X=\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(\mathcal O_Y[t]/(t^{19317}-u)\bigr)\longrightarrow Y
\]

is finite étale of degree \(19317\).  
Transitivity of the geometric monodromy group implies that the fibre over any geometric point of \(Y\) consists of exactly \(19317\) distinct geometric points.

Therefore  

\[
\boxed{19317.0000}.
\]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let D ⊂ ℙ² be the smooth conic given by the homogeneous equation x² + y² = z². Consider the family of lines ℓ_{k}: 3x + 4y + k z = 0 parametrized by the scalar k. Find the value of k for which the line ℓ_{k} is tangent to D. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Define the morphism f : ℙ¹ → ℙ¹ by f([s:t]) = [s^{x} : t^{x}]. Compute the degree of f by counting the number of points in a geometric generic fiber. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Consider a smooth plane curve C of degree y over the finite field 𝔽_{y^2}. Using the Lang–Weil estimate, give the main term q in the point count #C(𝔽_q). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

The line \(\ell_k : 3x+4y+kz=0\) meets the conic  

\[
D:\;x^{2}+y^{2}=z^{2}

in the points obtained by eliminating \(z\).  
From the line we have \(z =-\dfrac{3x+4y}{k}\) (for \(k\neq 0\)).  
Substituting in the conic gives  

\[
x^{2}+y^{2}= \frac{(3x+4y)^{2}}{k^{2}}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
k^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})-(3x+4y)^{2}=0 .
\]

Expanding,

\[
(k^{2}-9)x^{2}+(k^{2}-16)y^{2}-24xy=0 .
\]

This homogeneous quadratic in \(x,y\) represents a double line (i.e. the line is tangent) precisely when its discriminant vanishes:

\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
k^{2}-9 & -12\\[2pt]
-12 & k^{2}-16
\end{pmatrix}=0 .
\]

Hence  

\[
(k^{2}-9)(k^{2}-16)-144=0
\Longrightarrow k^{4}-25k^{2}=0
\Longrightarrow k^{2}(k^{2}-25)=0 .
\]

The non‑zero solutions are \(k=\pm5\).  
Taking the positive value (any choice is acceptable), we obtain  

\[
\boxed{5.0000}
\]

Let \(x=5\). The morphism  

\[
f:\mathbb P^{1}\longrightarrow\mathbb P^{1},
\qquad 
f([s:t])=[s^{5}:t^{5}]
\]

has degree equal to the number of points in a geometric generic fibre.  
For a generic point \([u:v]\in\mathbb P^{1}\) the equations  

\[
s^{5}= \lambda u,\qquad t^{5}= \lambda v
\]

have exactly five solutions for \([s:t]\) (up to the common scalar \(\lambda\)).  
Thus \(\deg f =5\), and  

\[
\boxed{5.0000}
\]

The Lang–Weil estimate for a smooth projective curve states  

\[
\#C(\mathbb F_{q}) = q + 1 + O(\sqrt{q}) ,
\]

where the leading (main) term is simply \(q\).  
Here \(q = y^{2}=5^{2}=25\).  Hence the main term is  

\[
\boxed{25.0000}

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the smooth conic D \subset \mathbb{P}^2 defined by the homogeneous equation x^2 + y^2 - z^2 = 0. Its dual curve D^\vee in the dual projective plane (with coordinates (a\!:\!b\!:\!c) corresponding to the line a x + b y + c z = 0) is given by a^2 + b^2 - c^2 = 0. Let the line \ell be defined by the coefficients (a,b,c) = (3,4,5). Compute the value of the dual equation a^2 + b^2 - c^2 at the point (3,4,5). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the symmetric matrix
\[ M = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x & 2 \\ x & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}. \]
Compute the determinant of M. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Let y = your answer to part (b). Consider the family of plane conics in \mathbb{P}^2 parametrized by t \in \mathbb{C} given by the quadratic form defined by the symmetric matrix
\[ M(t) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \frac{t\,y}{2} & 0 \\ \frac{t\,y}{2} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. \]
Using generic smoothness, determine the values of t for which the fiber is singular, and compute the product of those t values. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the projective plane \(\mathbb{P}^2\), a smooth conic (degree 2) and a smooth cubic curve (degree 3) intersect transversely. Using Bézout's theorem, how many intersection points (counted with multiplicity) do they have? Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Using the representation of plane conics as symmetric 3\times3 matrices, each point (in homogeneous coordinates) imposes one linear condition on the six independent entries of the matrix. Determine the dimension of the projective linear subspace of \(\mathbb{P}^5\) consisting of conics that pass through exactly x/2 of those intersection points (assume x is even). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Consider a finite étale morphism \(f : X \to \mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \{0,1,\infty\}\) of degree y whose geometric monodromy group acts transitively on the fiber over a geometric point. Using this transitivity, what is the cardinality of any geometric fiber of f? Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the smooth quadric surface X \subset \mathbb{P}^3 over the finite field \mathbb{F}_{13} defined by the homogeneous equation X_0 X_1 = X_2 X_3. This surface is geometrically irreducible of dimension 2 and degree 2. Using the Lang–Weil estimate, give the leading term of the point count #X(\mathbb{F}_{13}) and report it as a decimal rounded to 4 decimal places. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the univariate polynomials f(t) = t^2 + x and g(t) = t + 1 over \mathbb{Q}. Compute the resultant Res_{t}(f,g) to eliminate t, evaluate it using the numeric value of x, and give the resulting number rounded to 4 decimal places. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Examine the family of plane curves in \mathbb{P}^2 \times \mathbb{P}^1 given by the homogeneous equation F_s(X,Y,Z) = X^2 + Y^2 - (s - y) Z^2, where s is the coordinate on the base \mathbb{P}^1. Using generic smoothness, determine the value of the parameter s at which the fiber fails to be smooth, and output that value rounded to 4 decimal places inside \boxed{}. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.text: Consider the smooth cubic curve D ⊂ ℙ² given in affine coordinates (z=1) by y² = x³ - 3x + 2. For the one‑parameter family of lines ℓ_t: y = t·x + 1, determine the value of the parameter t for which ℓ_t is tangent to D. parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the morphism f: \mathbb{P}^1 \to \mathbb{P}^1 over an algebraically closed field given in affine coordinates by f(t) = t^3 - t. This map is finite and dominant. Compute the degree of f by counting the number of points in a geometric generic fiber. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Let f_p: X_p \to Y_p be the reduction modulo a prime p of the same morphism defined over \mathbb{Z}, which is finite étale away from the discriminant locus. Using the fact that the average size of the fibers f_p^{-1}(y) for y \in Y_p(\mathbb{F}_p) approaches the degree of f as p \to \infty, compute the limit \(\displaystyle \lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{1}{\#Y_p(\mathbb{F}_p)}\sum_{y\in Y_p(\mathbb{F}_p)}\#f_p^{-1}(y)\). Express your answer in terms of x and give the numeric value. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Consider the morphism g: \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C} defined by g(z) = z^{y}. The Jacobian determinant of g is J(z) = y\cdot z^{y-1}. Determine the number of points in \mathbb{C} where J(z) = 0. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

per_skill_role.parametrize_conics_by_symmetric_matrices: Part (a) asks to encode a given conic as a symmetric matrix with a fixed entry and output its determinant.
per_skill_role.compute_resultant_to_eliminate_variables: Part (b) uses the determinant from (a) as a coefficient in two binary quadratics and asks for their resultant.
per_skill_role.apply_monodromy_transitivity_to_constanc: Part (c) treats the resultant value as the degree of a finite étale cover with transitive monodromy, concluding the constant fiber size.

skill_chain_rationale: The output of part (a) (a determinant) supplies the coefficient x for the resultant in part (b); the resultant value y from part (b) becomes the degree of an étale cover used in part (c) to deduce fiber cardinality.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the conic in projective coordinates (x:y:z) given by 4x^2 + 2xy + y^2 - 2xz + 3yz + 5z^2 = 0. Represent this conic by a symmetric 3×3 matrix M such that the (1,1) entry of M equals 1. Compute the determinant of M. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the binary quadratics f(t) = t^2 + x t + 1 and g(t) = 2 t^2 - 3 t + x. Compute the resultant Res_{t}(f,g). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Suppose we have a finite étale morphism f : X \to \mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \{0,\infty\} of degree y, and the associated geometric monodromy group acts transitively on a geometric fiber. What is the cardinality of each geometric fiber of f? Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

Dividing by \(4\) makes the \((1,1)\) entry equal to \(1\):
\[

In \(\mathbb{P}^{2}\) Bézout’s theorem states that two projective plane curves of degrees \(d_{1}\) and \(d_{2}\) intersect in exactly \(d_{1}d_{2}\) points when counted with multiplicity, provided they have no common component.  
Here \(d_{1}=2\) (the conic) and \(d_{2}=3\) (the cubic). Because the intersection is transverse, each intersection point contributes multiplicity 1.  

\[
\#\text{intersection points}=2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

\boxed{6.0000}
\]

The morphism \(f:\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}\) given by \(f(t)=t^{x}=t^{6}\) has degree \(\deg(f)=x=6\).  

For a finite morphism of curves over a finite field, the average cardinality of a fiber over all \(\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\) points tends to the degree of the map as the field size grows, provided the characteristic does not divide the degree. Hence

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{1}{|\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})|}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}|f^{-1}(y)|
= \deg(f)=6 .
\]

\boxed{6.0000}
\]

The morphism \(g:\mathbb{A}^{1}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}\) is \(g(z)=z^{6}\).  
The Jacobian (derivative) is  

\[
g'(z)=6z^{5}.
\]

In characteristic \(p\neq 2,3\) (so \(6\neq 0\) in \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)), the map is étale at a point \(a\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\) exactly when \(g'(a)\neq 0\), i.e. when \(a^{5}\neq 0\). This holds for every non‑zero element of \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\); at \(a=0\) the derivative vanishes.

Thus, among the \(p\) points of \(\mathbb{A}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\), \(p-1\) are étale. The proportion is  

\[
\frac{p-1}{p}=1-\frac{1}{p}\xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{}1.
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Consider the finite morphism \(f:\mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}\to\mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}\) given on homogeneous coordinates by \([X:Z]\mapsto [X^5:Z^5]\). For each prime \(p\), let
\[ A(p)=\frac{1}{\#\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p)}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p)}\#f^{-1}(y).\]
Compute the limit \(\displaystyle\lim_{p\to\infty}A(p)\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Let x = your answer to part (a).  In the projective plane \(\mathbb{P}^2\) with homogeneous coordinates \((u:v:w)\), consider the symmetric matrix
\[ M = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \tfrac{x}{2} \\ 0 & \tfrac{x}{2} & 1 \end{pmatrix}.\]
The associated conic is defined by \([u\;v\;w]\,M\,[u\;v\;w]^T=0\).  Compute the determinant of \(M\).  Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b).  Let \(n\) be the nearest integer to \(|y|\).  Suppose \(g:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}\) is a finite étale cover of geometrically connected schemes over \(\mathbb{Z}\) whose geometric monodromy group acts transitively on the fiber over a geometric point and whose degree is \(n\).  What is the cardinality of each geometric fiber of \(g\)?  Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

For the map \([X:Z]\mapsto [X^{5}:Z^{5}]\) we work in the affine coordinate \(t=X/Z\).  
Over \(\mathbf{F}_{p}\) the map is \(t\mapsto t^{5}\).  

* The point at infinity maps to infinity, so the fibre over \(\infty\) has size \(1\).  
* The point \(0\) maps to \(0\); its fibre also has size \(1\).  
* For \(y\in\mathbf{F}_{p}^{\times}\) the equation \(t^{5}=y\) has either \(0\) or  
\(\gcd(5,p-1)\) solutions.  

Let \(d=\gcd(5,p-1)\).  
The homomorphism \(t\mapsto t^{5}\) from \(\mathbf{F}_{p}^{\times}\) (a cyclic group of order \(p-1\)) has kernel of size \(d\) and image of size \((p-1)/d\).  
Hence exactly \((p-1)/d\) non‑zero \(y\)’s have \(d\) preimages each.

Summing the fibre sizes:
\[
\sum_{y\in\mathbf{P}^{1}(\mathbf{F}_{p})}\#f^{-1}(y)
=1\;(\infty)+1\;(0)+d\cdot\frac{p-1}{d}=p+1 .
\]

Since \(\#\mathbf{P}^{1}(\mathbf{F}_{p})=p+1\),

\[
A(p)=\frac{p+1}{p+1}=1\qquad\text{for every prime }p .
\]

Thus  
\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the smooth conic D in \(\mathbb{P}^2\) given by the homogeneous equation \(x^2 + y^2 - z^2 = 0\). A line \(\ell\) in \(\mathbb{P}^2\) can be represented by its dual coordinates \((a,b,c)\) in the dual projective plane, i.e., \(\ell: a\,x + b\,y + c\,z = 0\). The dual curve \(D^\vee\) is defined by the same quadratic equation \(a^2 + b^2 - c^2 = 0\). For the line with coefficients \((a,b,c) = (3,4,5)\), compute the value of \(a^2 + b^2 - c^2\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the morphism \(f : \mathbb{P}^1 \to \mathbb{P}^1\) defined on homogeneous coordinates \([s:t]\) by \(f([s:t]) = [s^2 + x\,t^2 : t^2]\). This map is finite and dominant. Determine the degree of \(f\) by counting the number of points in a geometric generic fiber. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Let \(f(u,v) = u^2 + y\,v^2\) and \(g(u,v) = u + v\) be two homogeneous polynomials in variables \(u, v\) with coefficients depending on \(y\). Compute the resultant of \(f\) and \(g\) with respect to the variable \(u\), i.e., \(\operatorname{Res}_u(f,g)\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

For a generic point \(w\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{C})\) the equation \(z^{3}=w\) has three distinct solutions (the three cubic roots of \(w\)). Hence the geometric generic fibre consists of three points, so  

\[
\deg f = 3 .
\]

\[
\boxed{3.0000}
\]

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x=\deg f=3\).  
For each prime \(p\) the morphism over \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\) is finite of degree \(3\).  
The map fails to be étale only at the ramified points (e.g. \(0\) and \(\infty\)), which constitute a set of size bounded independently of \(p\). Consequently the average size of the fibre over \(\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\) satisfies  

\[
\frac{1}{\#\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\#f^{-1}(y)\;\longrightarrow\; \deg f = x
\qquad (p\to\infty).
\]

Thus  

\[
L = x = 3 .
\]

\[
\boxed{3.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Set \(y = L = 3\).  
The morphism \(g:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}\) is  

\[
g(z)=z^{\,y+1}=z^{4}.
\]

Its Jacobian (derivative) is  

\[
g'(z)=4z^{3}.
\]

The derivative vanishes exactly when \(z=0\). Hence there is a single point in the target where \(g\) is not étale.

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

**Part (a)**  

The morphism  

\[
f:\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb C}\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb C},
\qquad [s:t]\mapsto [s^{3}:t^{3}]
\]

is given in an affine chart \(t\neq 0\) by the map on the coordinate \(z=s/t\):

\[
z\;\longmapsto\;z^{3}.
\]

For a generic point \(y=[a:b]\in\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb C}\) (with \(a,b\neq 0\)), the fibre \(f^{-1}(y)\) is described by  

\[
\frac{s^{3}}{t^{3}}=\frac{a}{b}\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\Bigl(\frac{s}{t}\Bigr)^{3}=\frac{a}{b}.
\]

Since \(\mathbb C\) is algebraically closed, the equation \(w^{3}=a/b\) has exactly three distinct solutions for \(w=s/t\). Hence the geometric generic fibre consists of three points (counted without multiplicity).  

Thus  

\[
\deg f = 3.
\]

\[
\boxed{3.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x\) be the degree found in part (a); \(x=3\).  
Consider the same morphism defined over \(\mathbb Z\),

\[
f:\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb Z}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb Z},\qquad [s:t]\mapsto [s^{3}:t^{3}].
\]

For each prime \(p\) we may reduce modulo \(p\) and obtain a finite map  

\[
f_{p}:\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})\longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb F_{p}).
\]

A general fact about finite étale covers (or, more generally, about finite morphisms) is that the average size of the fibre over the \(\mathbb F_{p}\)-points converges to the degree of the map as \(p\to\infty\):

\[
\frac{1}{\#\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})}\#f_{p}^{-1}(y)\;\xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{}\;\deg f.
\]

Hence  

\[
L = \deg f = x = 3.
\]

\[
\boxed{3.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Set \(y\) to be the answer from part (b); \(y=3\).  
Define the complex map  

\[
g:\mathbb C\longrightarrow\mathbb C,\qquad g(z)=z^{\,y+1}=z^{4}.
\]

A map between complex manifolds is étale exactly where its Jacobian determinant (the complex derivative) is non‑zero.  

\[
g'(z)=\frac{d}{dz}z^{4}=4z^{3}.
\]

The derivative vanishes only at \(z=0\). The image of this point under \(g\) is \(g(0)=0\). Therefore the *target* point where \(g\) fails to be étale is the single point \(0\in\mathbb C\).

Hence the number of such points is  

\[
1.
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

**Part (a)**  

In \(\mathbb{P}^{2}\) Bézout’s theorem states that two plane curves of degrees \(d_{1}\) and \(d_{2}\) that share no common component intersect in exactly \(d_{1}d_{2}\) points, counted with multiplicity.  
Here \(d_{1}=2\) (the conic) and \(d_{2}=4\) (the quartic), so  

\[
\#(C_{2}\cap C_{4}) = 2\cdot 4 = 8 .
\]

\[
\boxed{8.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x\) be the answer from (a); thus \(x=8\).  
Take a smooth plane curve \(C\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\) of degree \(x=8\) and a point \(P\notin C\).  
The projection morphism  

\[
f:C\longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1},\qquad Q\mapsto \text{line }PQ
\]

has fibers given by the intersection of \(C\) with a line through \(P\).  
A line has degree 1, so by Bézout a generic line meets \(C\) in exactly \(\deg C = 8\) points (counted with multiplicity), and because \(C\) is smooth and the line is generic the intersection is transversal, giving 8 distinct points.  

Hence \(\deg f = 8\).

\[
\boxed{8.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

For the finite étale morphism \(f:C\to\mathbb{P}^{1}\) of degree \(d=8\), consider the average size of the fiber over \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-rational points of the base:

\[
\frac{1}{|\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})|}\sum_{t\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\bigl|f^{-1}(t)(\mathbb{F}_{p})\bigr|
   = \frac{|C(\mathbb{F}_{p})|}{p+1}.
\]

By the Weil bound for a smooth plane curve of degree 8, the genus is  

\[
g = \frac{(8-1)(8-2)}{2}=21,
\]

and  

\[
|C(\mathbb{F}_{p})| = p+1 - a_{p},\qquad |a_{p}|\le 2g\sqrt{p}=42\sqrt{p}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\frac{|C(\mathbb{F}_{p})|}{p+1}=1-\frac{a_{p}}{p+1}\xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{}1.
\]

Therefore the limiting average size of the fiber is \(1\).

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the smooth conic D in \(\mathbb{P}^2\) given by \(X^2 + Y^2 = Z^2\). Its dual curve \(D^\vee\) in the dual projective plane with coordinates \((A\!:\!B\!:\!C)\) is defined by \(A^2 + B^2 = C^2\). For the line \(\ell\): \(3X + 4Y + 5Z = 0\), compute the value of the left‑hand side of the dual equation at the point \((A,B,C) = (3,4,5)\). This value determines whether \(\ell\) is tangent to \(D\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Over the finite field \(\mathbb{F}_{101}\), consider the projective plane curve C defined by the homogeneous equation \(Y^2 Z = (2 + x) X^3 + Z^3\). Using the Lang–Weil estimate, approximate the number of \(\mathbb{F}_{101}\)-rational points on C by its leading term \(q^{\dim}\) (where \(\dim = 1\) for a curve). Compute this approximation and round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Suppose we have a finite étale morphism \(f : X \to Y\) defined over \(\mathbb{Z}\) such that for the prime \(p = 13\) we have \(#Y(\mathbb{F}_{13}) = p + 1\) and the total number of \(\mathbb{F}_{13}\)-rational points on \(X\) is exactly \(y\). Compute the average size of the fibers of \(f\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{13}\)-points of \(Y\), and deduce the degree \(\deg(f)\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the smooth conic D ⊂ ℙ² given by the homogeneous equation x² + y² − z² = 0. Let ℓ be the line with equation 3x + 4y − z = 0. Using the dual conic of D, evaluate the dual equation u² + v² − w² at the point (u,v,w) = (3,4,−1) that represents ℓ. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Define n = \lfloor x/5 \rfloor (the greatest integer ≤ x/5). Consider the morphism f : ℙ¹ → ℙ¹ which in the affine coordinate t is given by f(t) = t^{n} + x. Determine the degree of this finite map f. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Let y = your answer to part (b). Form the two univariate polynomials in the variable s

    f(s) = s² + y s + 1,
    g(s) = s³ + 2 s + y.

Compute the resultant Res_{s}(f, g) and give its numeric value. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

The geometric generic fiber of \(f\) is obtained by solving  

\[
t^{4}+t^{2}+1 = y
\]

over the algebraic closure of the function field \(\mathbb{Q}(y)\).  
This is a quartic polynomial in \(t\). Its derivative is  

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(t^{4}+t^{2}+1-y\bigr)=4t^{3}+2t = 2t\,(2t^{2}+1).
\]

A common root of the polynomial and its derivative would satisfy either  
\(t=0\) (giving \(y=1\)) or \(2t^{2}+1=0\) (giving \(y=3/4\)).  
These are isolated values of \(y\); for the *generic* point of \(\mathbb{A}^{1}\) the polynomial is separable, so it has **four distinct roots**.  

Hence the degree of \(f\) equals the number of points in the geometric generic fiber:

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x\) be the answer from part (a), i.e. \(x=4\).  
For a prime \(p\) (away from the discriminant values \(y=1,3/4\)), the reduction  

\[
f_{p} : \mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}} \longrightarrow \mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}},\qquad
t \mapsto t^{4}+t^{2}+1
\]

is a finite étale morphism. The average size of a fiber  

\[
\frac{1}{p}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{F}_{p}} \#f_{p}^{-1}(y)
\]

tends to the degree of the map as \(p\to\infty\). Therefore the limiting average fiber size equals the degree found in part (a):

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

The morphism  

\[
g : \mathbb{A}^{2}_{\mathbb{C}} \to \mathbb{A}^{2}_{\mathbb{C}},\qquad
(x,z) \mapsto (x^{2},\,z^{3})
\]

has Jacobian matrix  

\[
J_{g}=
\begin{pmatrix}
\frac{\partial (x^{2})}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial (x^{2})}{\partial z}\\[4pt]
\frac{\partial (z^{3})}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial (z^{3})}{\partial z}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2x & 0\\
0 & 3z^{2}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\det J_{g}= (2x)(3z^{2}) = 6\,x\,z^{2}.
\]

The determinant is non‑zero exactly when \(x\neq 0\) and \(z\neq 0\).  
Thus the étale locus is  

\[
U = \{(x,z)\in\mathbb{A}^{2}\mid x\neq 0,\;z\neq 0\}
      = (\mathbb{A}^{1}\!\setminus\!\{0\})\times(\mathbb{A}^{1}\!\setminus\!\{0\}).
\]

For a prime \(p\) (with \(p\neq 2,3\) so that \(6\) remains invertible), the number of \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-points in \(U\) is  

\[
(p-1)^{2},
\]

while the total number of points in \(\mathbb{A}^{2}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\) is \(p^{2}\).  
The proportion is therefore  

\[
\frac{(p-1)^{2}}{p^{2}} = \left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{2}=1-\frac{2}{p}+\frac{1}{p^{2}}
\longrightarrow 1\quad\text{as }p\to\infty .
\]

Hence the limiting proportion of points lying in the étale locus is  

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (a)**  

The morphism  

\[
f:\mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb Q}\longrightarrow \mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb Q},\qquad 
t\longmapsto t^{4}+t^{2}+1
\]

corresponds to the inclusion of function fields  

\[
\mathbb Q(s)\hookrightarrow \mathbb Q(t),\qquad s=t^{4}+t^{2}+1 .
\]

The degree of \(f\) is the degree of the field extension \(\mathbb Q(t)/\mathbb Q(s)\), which equals the degree of the minimal polynomial of \(t\) over \(\mathbb Q(s)\).  
Since the defining equation is \(t^{4}+t^{2}+1-s=0\), a monic polynomial of degree 4, and we are in characteristic 0 (hence separable), the generic fibre consists of **four distinct geometric points**.  

\[
\deg(f)=4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x\) be the answer from part (a); thus \(x=4\).  
For a prime \(p\) (away from the discriminant of \(t^{4}+t^{2}+1\)) we obtain a finite étale map  

\[
f_{p}:\mathbb A^{1}_{\mathbb F_{p}}\longrightarrow \mathbb A^{1}_{\mathbb F_{p}} .
\]

For any finite morphism the average cardinality of the fibres over \(\mathbb F_{p}\) satisfies  

\[
\frac{1}{p}\sum_{y\in\mathbb F_{p}} \#f_{p}^{-1}(y)=\deg(f_{p}) .
\]

Because reduction modulo \(p\) does not change the degree, \(\deg(f_{p})=\deg(f)=4\).  
Consequently, as \(p\to\infty\) the average fibre size tends to 4.

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

\[
t^{4}+t^{2}+1-s=0 .
\]

This polynomial is of degree 4 in \(t\) and is separable over a characteristic‑0 field (its discriminant is non‑zero). Hence the geometric generic fiber consists of 4 distinct points over \(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\).  

\[
\deg f = 4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x\) be the degree found in part (a), i.e. \(x=4\).  
For each prime \(p\) (away from the discriminant locus) we obtain a finite étale map  

\[
f_{p} : \mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}} \longrightarrow \mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}} .
\]

The average size of a fiber \(\#f_{p}^{-1}(y)\) over all \(y\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\) approaches the degree of the map as \(p\to\infty\). Consequently  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{1}{p}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}\#f_{p}^{-1}(y)=\deg f = 4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

The morphism \(g:\mathbb{A}^{2}_{\mathbb{C}}\to\mathbb{A}^{2}_{\mathbb{C}}\) is  
\[
g(x,z) = (x^{2},\,z^{3}).
\]

*Jacobian.*  

\[
J_g=\begin{pmatrix}
\frac{\partial (x^{2})}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial (x^{2})}{\partial z}\\[4pt]
\frac{\partial (z^{3})}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial (z^{3})}{\partial z}
\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}
2x & 0\\
0 & 3z^{2}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\det J_g = (2x)(3z^{2}) = 6\,x\,z^{2}.
\]

*Étale locus.*  
The determinant is non‑zero exactly when \(x\neq 0\) and \(z\neq 0\). Therefore the finite étale locus is  

\[
U = \{(x,z)\in\mathbb{A}^{2}\mid x\neq 0,\;z\neq 0\}.
\]

*Proportion over \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\).*  

Total points in \(\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}\): \(p^{2}\).  
Points with \(x\neq 0\) and \(z\neq 0\): \((p-1)^{2}\).  

Thus  

\[
\frac{\#U(\mathbb{F}_{p})}{p^{2}}=\frac{(p-1)^{2}}{p^{2}}=\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{2}=1-\frac{2}{p}+\frac{1}{p^{2}}.
\]

Taking \(p\to\infty\) gives the limiting proportion  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{\#U(\mathbb{F}_{p})}{p^{2}} = 1 .
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let \(q = 101\). Consider the smooth plane conic \(C \subset \mathbb{P}^2_{\mathbb{F}_q}\) defined by the homogeneous equation \(X_0^2 + X_1^2 + X_2^2 = 0\). Using the Lang–Weil estimate with the implied constant taken to be 1, approximate the number of \(\mathbb{F}_q\)-rational points on \(C\) by the expression \(q + 1 + \sqrt{q}\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the two homogeneous quadratics in variables \(u,v,w\):
\[ f(u,v,w) = u^2 + v^2 + w^2 - x\,u v, \]
\[ g(u,v,w) = u^2 - v w + x\,v^2. \]
Compute the resultant \(R(u,v) = \operatorname{Res}_w\bigl(f,g\bigr)\), which eliminates \(w\) and yields a polynomial in \(u, v\) (and the parameter \(x\)). Then evaluate this resultant at \(u = 1\) and \(v = 1\) to obtain a single numerical value. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Let y = your answer to part (b). Over the same finite field \(\mathbb{F}_{101}\), consider the family of plane curves in \(\mathbb{P}^2 \times \mathbb{A}^1\) given by
\[ F_t(u,v,w) = u^3 + v^3 + w^3 + y\,t\,u v w = 0, \]
where \(t\) is the coordinate on \(\mathbb{A}^1\). By generic smoothness, the morphism to the \(t\)-line is smooth (hence flat) over the dense open set where the fibers are smooth. Assuming \(y \neq 0\), the fibers are smooth precisely when \(t \neq 0\). Compute the proportion of \(t \in \mathbb{F}_{101}\) for which the fiber is smooth, i.e., the ratio of the number of smooth fibers to the total number of \(t\)-values. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the two homogeneous quadratics in variables \(u,v,w\):
\[ f(u,v,w) = u^2 + v^2 + w^2 - x\,u v, \]
\[ g(u,v,w) = u^2 - v w + x\,v^2. \]
Compute the resultant \(R(u,v) = \operatorname{Res}_w\bigl(f,g\bigr)\), which eliminates \(w\) and yields a polynomial in \(u, v\) (and the parameter \(x\)). Then evaluate this resultant at \(u = 1\) and \(v = 1\) to obtain a single numerical value. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Let y = your answer to part (b). Over the same finite field \(\mathbb{F}_{101}\), consider the family of plane curves in \(\mathbb{P}^2 \times \mathbb{A}^1\) given by
\[ F_t(u,v,w) = u^3 + v^3 + w^3 + y\,t\,u v w = 0, \]

calibration_attempts.text:
**Part (a)**  

The morphism  

\[
f:\mathbb P^{1}\longrightarrow \mathbb P^{1},\qquad f(t)=t^{5}
\]

is given in an affine chart by the polynomial \(t\mapsto t^{5}\).  
For a finite morphism of curves, the degree equals the number of points in a geometric generic fibre.  

The equation \(t^{5}=a\) (with \(a\) a generic point of the target) has exactly five distinct solutions in an algebraic closure, because the polynomial \(t^{5}-a\) is separable for generic \(a\).  

Hence  

\[
\deg f = 5 .
\]

\[
\boxed{5.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x\) be the answer from part (a), i.e. \(x=5\).  
Consider  

\[
g:\mathbb C\longrightarrow\mathbb C,\qquad g(z)=z^{x}-z = z^{5}-z .
\]

The Jacobian determinant of a holomorphic function of one complex variable is just its complex derivative:

\[
g'(z)=5z^{4}-1 .
\]

We need the points where this derivative vanishes:

\[
5z^{4}-1=0 \;\Longrightarrow\; z^{4}=\frac{1}{5}.
\]

The equation \(z^{4}=1/5\) has exactly four distinct complex solutions:

\[
z=\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{1/4}e^{i\pi k/2},\qquad k=0,1,2,3 .
\]

Thus the Jacobian vanishes at **four** points of \(\mathbb C\).

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Let \(y\) be the answer from part (b), i.e. \(y=4\).  
Define the subvariety  

\[
X=\{(w,t)\in\mathbb C^{2}\mid w^{2}=t^{y}-1\}
   =\{(w,t)\mid w^{2}=t^{4}-1\}.
\]

The projection  

\[
\pi:X\longrightarrow\mathbb C,\qquad \pi(w,t)=t
\]

has fibre over a point \(t_{0}\) given by  

\[
\pi^{-1}(t_{0})=\{w\in\mathbb C\mid w^{2}=t_{0}^{4}-1\}.
\]

* If \(t_{0}^{4}-1\neq0\), the fibre consists of two distinct reduced points \(w=\pm\sqrt{t_{0}^{4}-1}\); it is smooth and the morphism is flat there.  
* If \(t_{0}^{4}-1=0\), i.e. \(t_{0}^{4}=1\), then the fibre is defined by \(w^{2}=0\), a double point at \(w=0\). This fibre is singular (non‑reduced), and \(\pi\) fails to be flat at such \(t_{0}\).

The equation \(t_{0}^{4}=1\) has exactly four solutions in \(\mathbb C\):

\[
t_{0}=1,\; -1,\; i,\; -i .
\]

Hence there are **four** parameter values where \(\pi\) is not flat.

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

---

\[

\]

\]

Define

\[
t^{3}-t=a\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad t^{3}-t-a=0 .
\]
This is a cubic polynomial in \(t\). Over an algebraically closed field its generic fiber consists of three distinct roots (the discriminant of \(t^{3}-t-a\) is non‑zero for generic \(a\)). Hence the geometric generic fiber has **3 points**, which is precisely the degree of the morphism.

\[
g(t)=t^{x}-1 = t^{3}-1 .
\]

The Jacobian determinant of a morphism \(\mathbb{A}^{1}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}\) is just the derivative:
\[
\frac{dg}{dt}=3t^{2}.
\]
This vanishes exactly when \(3t^{2}=0\). Over characteristic \(0\) (or any characteristic not dividing \(3\)) this occurs only at \(t=0\).

Thus the complement of the étale locus (the set where the Jacobian vanishes) consists of a single point.

\[
t^{3}=b+1 .

\[

\]

\[

Let \([u:v]\) be a *geometric generic* point of the target, i.e. \(u\neq0\) and \(v\neq0\).  
We must solve  

\[
[s^{3}:t^{3}]=[u:v].
\]

Two homogeneous pairs are equal iff they differ by a non‑zero scalar \(\lambda\):

\[
(s^{3},t^{3})=\lambda (u,v),\qquad \lambda\neq0 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{s^{3}}{t^{3}}=\frac{u}{v}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Bigl(\frac{s}{t}\Bigr)^{3}= \frac{u}{v}.
\]

Over an algebraically closed field (e.g. \(\mathbb{C}\)) the equation
\(\xi^{3}=u/v\) has **three** distinct solutions \(\xi\).  
Each solution gives a distinct ratio \(s:t\), and scaling of \([s:t]\) does not produce new points.  

Therefore a generic fiber consists of three points, so  

\[
\deg f = 3.
\]

Let \(x\) be the answer from (a): \(x=3\).

\[
C:\; x X^{2}+Y Z = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; 3X^{2}+Y Z =0 .

\[
Q=[X\;Y\;Z]\;M\;
\begin{bmatrix}X\\Y\\Z\end{bmatrix},
\]

where \(M\) is a symmetric \(3\times3\) matrix.  
Matching coefficients:

* \(X^{2}\) term: coefficient \(3\) \(\Rightarrow M_{11}=3\).
* \(Y Z\) term: coefficient \(1\) \(\Rightarrow M_{23}=M_{32}= \tfrac12\) (each off‑diagonal entry is half the coefficient).
* All other coefficients are \(0\).

Thus, up to an overall scalar factor,  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
3 & 0 & 0\\[2pt]
0 & 0 & \tfrac12\\[2pt]
0 & \tfrac12 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The determinant is  

\[
\det M = 3\,
\det\!\begin{pmatrix}0 & \tfrac12\\[2pt]\tfrac12 & 0\end{pmatrix}
=3\,(0\cdot0-\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12)
=3\left(-\frac14\right)

Let \(y=4\). The family is  
\[

A point \([x:y:z]\) of a fibre is singular iff \(F_t=0\) and all three partial derivatives vanish:
\[
\begin{cases}

3x^{2}+4t\,x^{3}y^{4}z^{4}=0,\\
3y^{2}+4t\,x^{4}y^{3}z^{4}=0,\\
3z^{2}+4t\,x^{4}y^{4}z^{3}=0.
\end{cases}
\]

If any coordinate is zero, the corresponding derivative forces that coordinate to be zero as well, which would make the whole point zero—impossible in projective space. Hence a singular point must have \(x,y,z\neq0\). Dividing the derivative equations by the appropriate powers yields
\[

\]
so \(y=\zeta x,\;z=\omega x\) with \(\zeta^{3}=\omega^{3}=1\). Substituting into the derivative equations gives
\[

Plugging this into the original equation leads to
\[
\frac{9}{4}x^{3}=0,
\]
which forces \(x=0\), contradicting the assumption that all coordinates are non‑zero. Therefore **no** point \([x:y:z]\) satisfies the singularity conditions for any value of \(t\).

Consequently every fibre is smooth; the morphism \(\pi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb A^{1}\) is smooth over the whole base. The number of \(t\)-values that must be removed is therefore zero.

parts.text: In the projective plane \(\mathbb{P}^2\) over an algebraically closed field, a smooth conic (degree 2) and a smooth cubic curve (degree 3) intersect transversely. How many intersection points do they have counted with multiplicity? Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

This map is finite étale away from \(t = 0\). Using the fact that the average size of a fiber over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) approaches the degree of \(f\) as \(p \to \infty\), compute the limit of the average fiber size. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

Determine the proportion of \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-rational points of the target \(\mathbb{P}^1\) where the Jacobian does not vanish, in the limit as \(p \to \infty\). Here the smooth conic has degree \(2\) and the smooth cubic has degree \(3\). Hence  

\[
\#(C_{2}\cap C_{3}) = 2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

Rounded to four decimal places:

\[

\]

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x\) be the answer from part (a); thus \(x=6\).  
The morphism \(f:\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}}\) given on the affine chart by \(t\mapsto t^{x}=t^{6}\) has degree equal to the exponent, i.e. \(\deg f = x = 6\).

For a finite morphism of degree \(d\) the average size of a fiber over \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\) tends to \(d\) as \(p\to\infty\). Therefore  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\text{(average fiber size)} = \deg f = 6 .
\]

Rounded to four decimal places:

\[

\]

Now \(y\) is the answer from part (b); thus \(y = 6\).  
The morphism \(f:\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}\) over a field of characteristic \(p\) is still given by \(t\mapsto t^{6}\). Its Jacobian (derivative) on the affine chart is  

\[
J(t)=y\,t^{y-1}=6t^{5}.
\]

The Jacobian vanishes exactly when \(t=0\) (and, in homogeneous coordinates, also at the point at infinity). These two source points map to the two target points \(0\) and \(\infty\) in \(\mathbb{P}^{1}\).  

Hence the map is étale over all target points except these two. The number of \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-rational points of \(\mathbb{P}^{1}\) is \(p+1\). The proportion of points where the Jacobian does **not** vanish is  

\[
\frac{(p+1)-2}{p+1}= \frac{p-1}{p+1}\; \xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{}\; 1 .
\]

Rounded to four decimal places:

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

Using this transitivity, determine the number of points in any geometric fiber of f. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

For each prime \(p\) and each \(a\in\mathbf{F}_{p}\) the fiber  
\[
f^{-1}(a)=\{\,t\in\mathbf{F}_{p}\mid t^{4}+t+1=a\,\}
\]
is the set of solutions of the polynomial  
\(t^{4}+t+(1-a)=0\).  

If we count the total number of pairs \((t,a)\) with \(a=f(t)\) we obtain  

\[
\sum_{a\in\mathbf{F}_{p}} \#f^{-1}(a)=\#\{(t,a)\mid a=f(t)\}=p,
\]

because for each \(t\in\mathbf{F}_{p}\) there is exactly one \(a\) (namely \(a=f(t)\)).  
Hence the average number of \(\mathbf{F}_{p}\)-points in a fiber is  

\[
\frac{1}{p}\sum_{a\in\mathbf{F}_{p}}\#f^{-1}(a)=\frac{p}{p}=1 .
\]

The average does not depend on \(p\); therefore  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\text{average}=1 .
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x\) be the answer from part (a); \(x=1\).  
The conic in \(\mathbf{P}^{2}\) is  

\[
xX^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}=0 .
\]

Writing the quadratic form \(\;Q(X,Y,Z)=X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}\) as  

\[
\begin{bmatrix}X&Y&Z\end{bmatrix}
M
\begin{bmatrix}X\\Y\\Z\end{bmatrix}=0,
\]

the symmetric matrix \(M\) (taken with the obvious coefficients) is  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its determinant is  

\[
\det(M)=1\cdot1\cdot1=1 .
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Let \(y\) be the answer from part (b); \(y=1\).  
A finite étale cover \(f\colon X\to\mathbf{P}^{1}\) of degree \(y\) has exactly \(y\) points in each geometric fiber, and transitivity of the monodromy group forces every geometric fiber to have the same size.  

Thus each geometric fiber contains  

\[
y=1
\]

point.

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

ANSWERS: {"a": "1.0000", "b": "1.0000", "c": "1.0000"}

**Part (a)**  

For a fixed prime \(p\) and \(a\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\) the fiber is  

\[
f^{-1}(a)=\{t\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\mid t^{4}+t+1 = a\}.
\]

The number of points in this fiber is  

\[
N_a=\#\{t\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\mid t^{4}+t+(1-a)=0\}.
\]

If we sum \(N_a\) over all \(a\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\) we simply count the pairs \((t,a)\) with
\(a=f(t)\):

\[
\sum_{a\in\mathbb{F}_{p}} N_a = \#\{(t,a)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}\mid a = t^{4}+t+1\}
= \#\{t\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\}=p .
\]

Hence the average number of \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-points in a fiber is  

\[
\frac{1}{p}\sum_{a} N_a = \frac{p}{p}=1 .
\]

For all sufficiently large primes (away from the finitely many primes where the map fails to be étale) this average is exactly \(1\); therefore  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\text{average}=1 .
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Insert the value from part (a): \(x=1\).  
The conic in \(\mathbb{P}^{2}\) is  

\[
X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}=0 .
\]

Writing it as \(v^{\mathsf T} M v =0\) with \(v=(X,Y,Z)^{\mathsf T}\) gives a diagonal matrix  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its determinant is  

\[
\det(M)=1\cdot 1\cdot 1 = 1 .
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

Determine the value of the parameter k for which C_k is tangent to D.  Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

Assuming f is finite étale away from its discriminant, compute the limiting average size of the fiber f^{-1}(y) for y \in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p) as p \to \infty.  Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

After obtaining the resultant R(z), evaluate it at z = 1.  Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

The conic \(C_k\) and the cubic \(D\) intersect tangentially when there exists a point \((x:y:z)\neq(0,0,0)\) satisfying  

\[
\begin{cases}
F(x,y,z)=x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}-3xyz=0,\\[2pt]
G(x,y,z)=x^{2}+y^{2}+kz^{2}=0,
\end{cases}
\]

and for which the gradients are linearly dependent:
\[
\nabla F=\lambda \nabla G .
\]

Writing \(a=x/y,\;b=z/y\;(y\neq0)\) and eliminating the variables gives the system  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a^{2}+1+k b^{2}&=0,\\
a^{3}+1+b^{3}-3ab&=0,\\
(1+b)a^{2}-a-b&=0,\\
b^{2}-a&=k b(1-ab).
\end{aligned}
\]

From \((1+b)a^{2}-a-b=0\) we obtain two branches:
\[
a=1\qquad\text{or}\qquad a=-\frac{b}{1+b}.
\]

The branch \(a=1\) leads to the cubic equation \(b^{3}-3b+2=0\), whose real solutions are \(b=1\) and \(b=-2\).  
Correspondingly

* for \(b=1\): \(k=-\dfrac{2}{1^{2}}=-2\);
* for \(b=-2\): \(k=-\dfrac{2}{(-2)^{2}}=-\dfrac12\).

Both values give a genuine tangency point \((1:1:1)\) and \((1:1:-2)\) respectively.  
Choosing the integer value (the simplest one) we take  

\[
\boxed{-2.0000}

The morphism \(f:\mathbf P^{1}\to\mathbf P^{1}\) is \(f(t)=t^{2}+x\).

\[
\#f^{-1}(y)=\#\{t\in\mathbf F_{p}\mid t^{2}=y-x\}
           =1+\chi(y-x),
\]

where \(\chi\) is the Legendre symbol.  
Averaging over all \(y\in\mathbf F_{p}\),

\[
\frac{1}{p}\sum_{y\in\mathbf F_{p}}(1+\chi(y-x))
   =1+\frac{1}{p}\sum_{a\in\mathbf F_{p}}\chi(a)=1,
\]

because \(\sum_{a\in\mathbf F_{p}}\chi(a)=0\).

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

is the limiting average size of the fibre.

Now \(y=1\).  Consider  

\[

g(x,z)=x^{2}-4z^{2}+1 .

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{x}(f,g)=(z^{2}-(-4z^{2}+1))^{2}=(5z^{2}-1)^{2}.
\]

Evaluating at \(z=1\),

\[
R(1)=(5\cdot1-1)^{2}=4^{2}=16 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{16.0000}
\]

**Part (b)**  

Now \(x=3\). Over \(\mathbb{F}_{7}\) the morphism \(g:\mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{7}}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{7}}\) is \(t\mapsto t^{3}\).  
Its Jacobian (derivative) is  

\[
g'(t)=3t^{2}.
\]

The map is étale at points where \(g'(t)\neq 0\) in \(\mathbb{F}_{7}\).  
Since \(3\neq 0\) in \(\mathbb{F}_{7}\), the condition reduces to \(t^{2}\neq 0\), i.e. \(t\neq 0\).  
There are \(7-1=6\) non‑zero elements of \(\mathbb{F}_{7}\). Thus the number of \(\mathbb{F}_{7}\)-points where \(g\) is étale is  

\[
y = 6.
\]

\[
\boxed{6.0000}
\]

**Part (c)**

For a finite étale morphism \(h:X\to Y\) between smooth, connected varieties over an algebraically closed field, all geometric fibers have the same cardinality (the degree of the covering). If one geometric fiber consists of \(y=6\) points, then every geometric fiber consists of exactly 6 points.

\[
\boxed{6.0000}
\]

**Part (a)**  

The morphism  

\[
f:\mathbb{P}^{1}\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1},\qquad t\longmapsto t^{3}
\]

is given in the affine chart \( \mathbb{A}^{1}\subset\mathbb{P}^{1}\) by the polynomial \(t^{3}\).  
For a dominant morphism of curves the degree equals the number of points in a *geometric generic fibre* (counted with multiplicity).  

A generic point of the target has coordinate \(s\) that is transcendental over the base field. Solving \(t^{3}=s\) gives the three distinct solutions  

\[
t=\zeta_{1}s^{1/3},\; \zeta_{2}s^{1/3},\; \zeta_{3}s^{1/3},
\]

where \(\zeta_{i}\) are the three cubic roots of unity in an algebraic closure. Hence the generic fibre consists of **3** points (each with multiplicity 1).  

\[
\boxed{3.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

From part (a) we have \(x=3\). Over the finite field \(\mathbb{F}_{7}\) the morphism  

\[
g:\mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{7}}\longrightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{7}},\qquad t\longmapsto t^{3}
\]

is a polynomial map.  
For a morphism of one‑dimensional affine varieties the Jacobian determinant is simply the derivative:

\[
g'(t)=\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(t^{3}\bigr)=3t^{2}.
\]

In characteristic \(7\) the coefficient \(3\) is non‑zero, so \(g'(t)=0\) iff \(t^{2}=0\), i.e. iff \(t=0\).

Thus \(g\) is étale at every \(\mathbb{F}_{7}\)-point except \(t=0\).  
\(\mathbb{A}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{7})\) has \(7\) points \(\{0,1,\dots ,6\}\). Removing the single non‑étale point leaves

\[
7-1 = 6
\]

étale points.

\[
\boxed{6.0000}
\]

For a finite étale morphism \(h:X\to Y\) between smooth, connected varieties over an algebraically closed field, the étale property implies that all geometric fibres have the same cardinality, namely the *degree* of the morphism.  
If the fibre over one geometric point consists of \(y\) points, monodromy transitivity forces every geometric fibre to consist of exactly the same number of points.

Hence every geometric fibre of \(h\) contains

\[
y = 6
\]

points.

\[
\boxed{6.0000}
\]

**Part (a)**  

For a morphism \(f:\mathbb P^{1}\to\mathbb P^{1}\) given by a rational function  
\[
t\longmapsto \frac{t^{3}-2t+1}{t^{2}+1},
\]
the degree equals the maximum of the degrees of the numerator and denominator after cancelling any common factor.  

- \(\deg(t^{3}-2t+1)=3\)  
- \(\deg(t^{2}+1)=2\)  

The two polynomials have no common root (they do not share the factors \(t\pm i\) over \(\mathbb C\)), so no cancellation occurs. Hence  

\[
\deg f=\max\{3,2\}=3.
\]

\[
\boxed{3.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

For a finite morphism of curves, the average cardinality of the fibers over \(\mathbb F_{p}\)-rational points tends to the degree of the morphism as \(p\to\infty\).  
Thus the limiting average fiber size is the same number obtained in part (a):

\[
\boxed{3.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Set \(y=3\) (the answer from part (b)).  
The map \(g:\mathbb A^{2}_{\mathbb F_{7}}\to\mathbb A^{2}_{\mathbb F_{7}}\) is  

\[
g(u,v)=\bigl(u^{2}+3v,\;v^{2}\bigr).
\]

*Jacobian determinant.*

\[
J(u,v)=\det\begin{pmatrix}
\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(u^{2}+3v) & \frac{\partial}{\partial v}(u^{2}+3v)\\[4pt]
\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(v^{2}) & \frac{\partial}{\partial v}(v^{2})
\end{pmatrix}
=\det\begin{pmatrix}
2u & 3\\
0 & 2v
\end{pmatrix}= (2u)(2v)-3\cdot0 =4uv.
\]

In \(\mathbb F_{7}\) the scalar \(4\) is non‑zero, so \(J(u,v)\neq0\) exactly when \(uv\neq0\); i.e. both coordinates are non‑zero.

*Open subset where the Jacobian is non‑zero.*

\[
U=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb F_{7}^{2}\mid u\neq0,\;v\neq0\}= \mathbb F_{7}^{\times}\times\mathbb F_{7}^{\times}.
\]

*Number of \(\mathbb F_{7}\)-rational points in \(U\).*

\[
|U|=(7-1)\times(7-1)=6\cdot6=36.
\]

\[
\boxed{36.0000}
\]

---

Since the numerator and denominator have no common factor (the roots of \(t^{2}+1\) are \(\pm i\), and neither satisfies \(t^{3}-2t+1=0\)), the degree of the map equals the larger of the two degrees:

\[

Using Bézout's theorem, determine the total number of intersection points counted with multiplicity. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

Consider a smooth projective surface \(X \subset \mathbb{P}^3\) defined over the finite field \(\mathbb{F}_{11}\), which is geometrically irreducible, has dimension 2 and degree equal to x. Apply the Lang–Weil estimate to approximate the number of \(\mathbb{F}_{11}\)-rational points on \(X\) by its leading term. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

\[f(u,v,w) = w^2 + v\,w + y\,u^2,\]
\[g(u,v,w) = w^2 + u\,w + y\,v^2.\]

Compute the resultant of \(f\) and \(g\) with respect to \(w\), then evaluate the resulting expression at \(u = 1\) and \(v = 2\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

In \(\mathbb{P}^{2}\) the intersection number of a curve of degree \(d_{1}\) with a curve of degree \(d_{2}\) is \(d_{1}d_{2}\) (Bézout).  
Here \(d_{1}=2\) (conic) and \(d_{2}=3\) (cubic), and the intersection is transverse, so each point has multiplicity 1.  

\[
\#\text{intersection points}=2\cdot3=6 .
\]

\[
\boxed{6.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x\) be the degree from part (a), i.e. \(x=6\).  
For a smooth projective surface \(X\) of dimension \(2\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\) the Lang–Weil estimate gives  

\[
\#X(\mathbb{F}_{q}) = q^{2}+O(q^{3/2}),
\]

so the leading term is \(q^{2}\).  
Here \(q=11\), thus  

\[
\#X(\mathbb{F}_{11}) \approx 11^{2}=121 .
\]

\[
\boxed{121.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Set \(y = 121\).  
The two homogeneous quadratics in \(w\) are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(u,v,w) &= w^{2}+v w+121\,u^{2},\\
g(u,v,w) &= w^{2}+u w+121\,v^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Write them as polynomials in \(w\):
\[
f = w^{2}+v w+121u^{2},\qquad 
g = w^{2}+u w+121v^{2}.
\]

For two quadratics \(a_{2}w^{2}+a_{1}w+a_{0}\) and \(b_{2}w^{2}+b_{1}w+b_{0}\) the resultant is  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{w}(f,g)=
a_{2}^{2}b_{0}^{2}-a_{2}a_{1}b_{1}b_{0}+a_{2}a_{0}b_{1}^{2}
-a_{1}^{2}b_{2}b_{0}+a_{1}a_{0}b_{2}b_{1}-a_{0}^{2}b_{2}^{2}.
\]

With \(a_{2}=b_{2}=1,\;a_{1}=v,\;b_{1}=u,\;a_{0}=121u^{2},\;b_{0}=121v^{2}\) this simplifies to  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{w}(f,g)=
121^{2}(v^{2}-u^{2})^{2}-121\,v\,(u-v)(v^{2}-u^{2})+121\,u^{2}(u-v)^{2}.
\]

Evaluating at \(u=1,\;v=2\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
v^{2}-u^{2} &= 4-1 = 3,\\
u-v &= -1,
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{w}(f,g)\big|_{u=1,v=2}
=121\bigl[121\cdot3^{2}+6+1\bigr]
=121\cdot1096
=132\,616.
\]

\[
\boxed{132616.0000}
\]

\[

A cubic equation over \(\mathbb{C}\) has three distinct roots, so there are three points where the Jacobian (the derivative) vanishes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the smooth projective curve X ⊂ ℙ² defined over an algebraically closed field by the affine equation y² = x³ + x + 1, and let Y = ℙ¹. Let f : X → Y be the morphism given by the projection onto the x‑coordinate (i.e., f(x,y) = x). Compute the degree of f by counting the number of points in a geometric generic fiber. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Using the Lang–Weil estimate for a geometrically irreducible projective curve of dimension 1 and degree x over the finite field \mathbb{F}_{11}, the error term in the point count is at most x·11^{1/2}. Compute the numerical value of this error bound E = x·\sqrt{11} and round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). For the same morphism f : X → \mathbb{P}¹, consider the finite field \mathbb{F}_{11}. The set \mathbb{P}¹(\mathbb{F}_{11}) has 11 + 1 = 12 points. Using the worst‑case estimate that #X(\mathbb{F}_{11}) \le 11 + y, compute the maximal possible average size of a fiber of f over \mathbb{F}_{11}, namely A = (11 + y) / 12. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

Its dual curve D^∨ is defined by a² + b² - c² = 0 in the dual projective plane (ℙ²)^∨, where (a:b:c) corresponds to the line a x + b y + c z = 0. For each prime \(p\),

\[
\#Y(\mathbb{F}_p)=\#\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_p)=p+1 .

The sum  

\[
\sum_{y\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_p)}\#f^{-1}(y)
\]

counts every \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-rational point of the source \(\mathbb{P}^{1}\) exactly once, because each rational point of \(X=\mathbb{P}^{1}\) maps to a unique \(y\). Hence  

\[
\sum_{y\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_p)}\#f^{-1}(y)=\#X(\mathbb{F}_p)=p+1 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
A_p=\frac{1}{p+1}\,(p+1)=1\qquad\text{for every prime }p,
\]

and  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}A_p = 1 .
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

Insert \(x=1\) into  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 0 & \tfrac12\\
0 & \tfrac12 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

\(M\) is block‑diagonal with a \(1\times1\) block \([1]\) (rank 1) and a \(2\times2\) block  

\[
\begin{pmatrix}0&\tfrac12\\[2pt]\tfrac12&0\end{pmatrix},
\]

whose determinant is \(-\tfrac14\neq0\), so this block has rank 2.  
Hence  

\[
\operatorname{rank}(M)=1+2=3 .
\]

\[
\boxed{3.0000}
\]

**Part (a)**  

For \(f(t)=t^{5}\) we have \(\#Y(\mathbf{F}_{p})=\#\mathbf{P}^{1}(\mathbf{F}_{p})=p+1\).

For a given \(y\in\mathbf{P}^{1}(\mathbf{F}_{p})\) the fibre \(\#f^{-1}(y)\) is:

* \(y=\infty\): one point \((t=\infty)\);
* \(y=0\): one point \((t=0)\);
* \(y\neq 0,\infty\): the equation \(t^{5}=y\) in \(\mathbf{F}_{p}^{\times}\).

If \(5\nmid(p-1)\) the map \(t\mapsto t^{5}\) is a bijection on \(\mathbf{F}_{p}^{\times}\); each non‑zero \(y\) has exactly one preimage.  
If \(5\mid(p-1)\) the map is \(5\)-to‑\(1\) onto the subgroup of fifth powers; there are \((p-1)/5\) such \(y\) each with \(5\) preimages, giving a total contribution \((p-1)/5\cdot5=p-1\).

In either case  

\[
\sum_{y\in\mathbf{P}^{1}(\mathbf{F}_{p})}\#f^{-1}(y)=1+1+(p-1)=p+1 .
\]

Hence  

\[
A_{p}= \frac{p+1}{p+1}=1\qquad\text{for all }p\neq5,
\]

and therefore  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}A_{p}=1 .
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}

parts.text: In the projective plane \(\mathbb{P}^2\) over an algebraically closed field, consider a smooth quartic curve (degree 4) and a line (degree 1) that intersect transversely. How many intersection points (counted with multiplicity) do they have? Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider a smooth projective plane curve of degree x over the finite field \(\mathbb{F}_{101}\). The Weil bound (a consequence of the Lang–Weil estimate) states that the number of \(\mathbb{F}_{101}\)-rational points satisfies \(|\#C(\mathbb{F}_{101}) - (101+1)| \le (x-1)(x-2)\sqrt{101}\). Compute the maximal possible number of \(\mathbb{F}_{101}\)-rational points on such a curve, i.e., \(101+1 + (x-1)(x-2)\sqrt{101}\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Consider the morphism \(f : X \to \mathbb{A}^1_{\mathbb{F}_{101}}\) defined in part (b), where the base \(\mathbb{A}^1(\mathbb{F}_{101})\) has exactly 101 rational points. By the generic smoothness theorem, the morphism is smooth, hence flat, over a dense open subset of the base; consequently it can fail to be flat over at most \(\lfloor y \rfloor\) points of the base. Compute the minimum number of \(\mathbb{F}_{101}\)-rational points of the base over which \(f\) is guaranteed to be flat, i.e., \(\max\bigl(0,\,101 - \lfloor y \rfloor\bigr)\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

The Jacobian matrix of  

\[
f(x,y)=\bigl(x^{2}+y,\;y^{2}+x\bigr)
\]

is  

\[
J_f(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^{2}+y) & \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^{2}+y)\\[2pt]
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(y^{2}+x) & \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(y^{2}+x)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2x & 1\\
1 & 2y
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\det J_f(x,y)= (2x)(2y)-1 =4xy-1 .
\]

At the point \((2,1)\),

\[
\det J_f(2,1)=4\cdot2\cdot1-1=8-1=7.
\]

\[
\boxed{7.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Take \(x=7\).  
The homogeneous quadratic form  

\[
Q(X,Y,Z)=7X^{2}+4XY+3Y^{2}+2YZ+4Z^{2}
\]

has the symmetric matrix (ordering the variables as \(X,Y,Z\))

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
7 & 2 & 0\\
2 & 3 & 1\\
0 & 1 & 4
\end{pmatrix},
\]
because the off‑diagonal entries are half the coefficients of the mixed terms.

The determinant is  

\[
\det M = 7\begin{vmatrix}3&1\\1&4\end{vmatrix}
        -2\begin{vmatrix}2&1\\0&4\end{vmatrix}
        +0\cdot(\dots)
      =7(12-1)-2(8)=7\cdot11-16=77-16=61.
\]

\[
\boxed{61.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Let \(y=61\).  
Consider  

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(s,t)&=61\,s^{2}+5\,s t+2\,t^{2},\\
g(s,t)&=3\,s^{2}+61\,s t+4\,t^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Treating \(t\) as a parameter, the Sylvester matrix for the resultant with respect to \(s\) is  

\[
S=\begin{pmatrix}
61 & 5t & 2t^{2} & 0\\
0  & 61 & 5t    & 2t^{2}\\
3  & 61t& 4t^{2}& 0\\
0  & 3  & 61t   & 4t^{2}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Factoring out the powers of \(t\) (each row contributes the appropriate factor) shows that the determinant is \(t^{4}\) times a constant.  Setting \(t=1\) (i.e. evaluating the constant factor) gives  

\[
\det S\big|_{t=1}=434\,656.
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{s}(f,g)=434656.
\]

\[
\boxed{434656.0000}
\]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the morphism \(f : X \to Y\) where \(X \subset \mathbb{P}^2\) is the smooth cubic curve defined by the homogeneous equation \(X_0^3 + X_1^3 + X_2^3 = 0\) and \(Y = \mathbb{P}^1\) with homogeneous coordinates \([s:t]\). The morphism is given by \([X_0 : X_1 : X_2] \mapsto [X_0 : X_1]\). This map is finite and dominant. Compute the degree of \(f\), i.e., the number of points in a geometric generic fiber. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the morphism \(g : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}\) defined by \(g(z) = z^{2} - x\). Determine the point \(y_{0}\) in the target where \(g\) fails to be étale (i.e., where the Jacobian determinant vanishes). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Let y = your answer to part (b). Consider the homogeneous polynomials in variables \(u,v,w\):
\[ f(u,v,w) = u^{2} + y\,v\,w, \qquad g(u,v,w) = v^{2} + w^{2}. \]
Compute the resultant of \(f\) and \(g\) with respect to the variable \(w\), obtaining a polynomial in \(u\) and \(v\) (which still depends on the numeric parameter \(y\)). Then evaluate this resultant at \(u = 1\) and \(v = 1\) to obtain a single real number. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

For a point \([s:t]\in \mathbb P^{1}\) the fibre of \(f\) consists of points \([X_{0}:X_{1}:X_{2}]\) on the cubic with \([X_{0}:X_{1}]=[s:t]\).  
Write \(X_{0}=s\lambda,\;X_{1}=t\lambda\) for some \(\lambda\neq 0\).  
Plugging into the cubic equation gives  

\[
(s\lambda)^{3}+(t\lambda)^{3}+X_{2}^{3}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
X_{2}^{3}= -\lambda^{3}(s^{3}+t^{3}).
\]

Thus \(X_{2}= \lambda\mu\) where \(\mu^{3}=-(s^{3}+t^{3})\).  
The three cube‑roots \(\mu\) give three distinct points of the fibre, except when
\(s^{3}+t^{3}=0\) (a special locus). Hence the generic fibre contains **three** points.

\[
\boxed{3.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x=3.0000\). The map \(g:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\) is  

\[
g(z)=z^{2}-x = z^{2}-3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the smooth cubic curve D in the projective plane given by the homogeneous equation X^3 + Y^3 + Z^3 = 0. Let \ell_t be the line with equation X + Y + t Z = 0, where t is a real parameter. Using the dual curve D^\vee, determine the value(s) of t for which \ell_t is tangent to D. If multiple values exist, give the smallest positive one. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the morphism f_x : \mathbb{P}^1 \to \mathbb{P}^1 defined in homogeneous coordinates by f_x([s:t]) = [s^3 + x s t^2 : t^3]. Compute the degree of this finite map by counting the points in a geometric generic fiber. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Let f(u) = u^2 + y u + 1 and g(u) = 2u^2 - 5u + y be two quadratic polynomials in the variable u. Compute the resultant Res_u(f,g), which eliminates u and yields a condition on y. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

The line \(\ell_t\) is given by \(X+Y+tZ=0\).  
On the affine chart \(Z=1\) we have \(X=-Y-t\). Substituting into the cubic  

\[
X^{3}+Y^{3}+Z^{3}=0
\]

gives  

\[
(-Y-t)^{3}+Y^{3}+1=0\Longrightarrow -3tY^{2}-3t^{2}Y-t^{3}+1=0 .
\]

Thus the intersection of \(\ell_t\) with \(D\) in this chart is described by the quadratic  

\[
-3tY^{2}-3t^{2}Y-(t^{3}-1)=0 .
\]

The line is tangent exactly when this quadratic has a double root, i.e. when its discriminant vanishes:

\[
\Delta = (-3t^{2})^{2}-4(-3t)(-t^{3}+1)=9t^{4}-12t^{4}+12t=12t-3t^{4}=3t\,(4-t^{3}) .
\]

Hence \(\Delta=0\) gives \(t=0\) or \(t^{3}=4\).  
The smallest **positive** solution is  

\[
t=4^{1/3}=1.587401051\ldots\;\approx\;1.5874 .
\]

\[
\boxed{1.5874}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x=1.5874\). The morphism  

\[
f_{x}\bigl([s:t]\bigr)=\bigl[s^{3}+xst^{2}:t^{3}\bigr]
\]

in the affine coordinate \(u=s/t\) becomes the rational function  

\[
\phi(u)=\frac{s^{3}+xst^{2}}{t^{3}}=u^{3}+xu .
\]

For a generic value \(y\in\mathbb{P}^{1}\) the fibre is obtained from  

\[
u^{3}+xu=y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u^{3}+xu-y=0,
\]

a cubic equation in \(u\).  For generic \(y\) the cubic has three distinct solutions (counted with multiplicity), so the map is finite of degree \(3\).

\[
\boxed{3.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Now \(y=3\).  

\[
f(u)=u^{2}+yu+1=u^{2}+3u+1,\qquad 
g(u)=2u^{2}-5u+y=2u^{2}-5u+3 .
\]

The resultant \(\operatorname{Res}_{u}(f,g)\) is the determinant of the Sylvester matrix  

\[
\begin{vmatrix}
1 & 3 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 3 & 1\\
2 & -5 & 3 & 0\\
0 & 2 & -5 & 3
\end{vmatrix}=155 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{155.0000}
\]

---

parts.text: Consider the smooth cubic curve D in the projective plane given by the homogeneous equation X^3 + Y^3 + Z^3 = 0. Let \ell_t be the line with equation X + Y + t Z = 0, where t is a real parameter. Using the dual curve D^\vee, determine the value(s) of t for which \ell_t is tangent to D. If multiple values exist, give the smallest positive one. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

Compute the degree of this finite map by counting the points in a geometric generic fiber. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the two homogeneous quadratic polynomials in variables \(u\) and \(v\):

\[f(u,v) = x\,u^{2} + 2\,u v + 3\,v^{2},\qquad g(u,v) = 4\,u^{2} + 5\,u v + 6\,v^{2}.\]

Compute the resultant of \(f\) and \(g\) with respect to the variable \(u\), thereby eliminating \(u\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Using the transitivity of the geometric monodromy group, determine how many points lie in a geometric fiber of \(f\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

The cubic curve  

\[
D:\;Y^{2}Z = X^{3}-XZ^{2}
\]

A projective line through \(P=(0\!:\!1\!:\!0)\) has equation  

\[
\alpha X+\gamma Z =0\qquad (\beta=0\text{ because }P\in L).
\]

If \(\gamma\neq0\) we may write it as \(X=\lambda Z\) with \(\lambda\in\mathbf{P}^{1}\); the case \(\gamma=0\) gives the line at infinity \(Z=0\).

*Intersection with \(D\).*  
Insert \(X=\lambda Z\) into the equation of \(D\):

\[
Y^{2}Z = (\lambda Z)^{3}-(\lambda Z)Z^{2}=Z^{3}(\lambda^{3}-\lambda).
\]

For \(Z\neq0\) (the affine chart \(Z=1\)) this becomes  

\[
y^{2}= \lambda^{3}-\lambda .
\]

Thus the vertical line \(x=\lambda\) meets \(D\) at the points \((\lambda,\pm\sqrt{\lambda^{3}-\lambda})\).  
The line is **tangent** when the two intersection points coincide, i.e. when  

\[
\lambda^{3}-\lambda =0\;\Longrightarrow\;\lambda(\lambda^{2}-1)=0,
\]

giving \(\lambda=0,\,1,\,-1\).  
For each of these three values the vertical line \(x=\lambda\) is tangent to \(D\) at the affine point \((\lambda,0)\).

*The line at infinity.*  
The line \(Z=0\) passes through \(P\) and meets \(D\) only at \(P\) with intersection multiplicity 3 (a flex), so it is also tangent at \(P\).

Hence there are exactly  

\[
3\text{ (vertical tangents)}+1\text{ (the line at infinity)}=4

distinct projective lines through \(P\) that are tangent to \(D\).

parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Using this value, form the symmetric matrix M = [[x,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,-2]], which represents a plane conic. Compute the absolute value of the determinant of M. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Define two binary quadratic forms in variables u and v: f(u,v)=u^2 + y*u*v + v^2 and g(u,v)=2*u^2 + (y-1)*u*v + 3*v^2. Compute the resultant Res_u(f,g) using the formula a0*b2 - a1*b1 + a2*b0, where a0,a1,a2 are the coefficients of f and b0,b1,b2 are those of g. Report the resultant value. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

The morphism \([s:t]\mapsto [s^{3}:t^{3}]\) raises each homogeneous coordinate to the third power.

\[
\deg f = 3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{3.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Insert \(x=3.0000\) into  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
x & 0 & 0\\[2pt]
0 & 1 & 0\\[2pt]
0 & 0 & -2
\end{pmatrix}
=\operatorname{diag}(3,1,-2).
\]

\[
\det M = 3\cdot 1\cdot (-2) = -6,\qquad |\det M| = 6.
\]

\[
\boxed{6.0000}
\]

Let \(y = 6.0000\).  

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(u,v) &= u^{2}+yuv+v^{2}=1\cdot u^{2}+6\cdot uv+1\cdot v^{2},\\
g(u,v) &= 2u^{2}+(y-1)uv+3v^{2}=2\cdot u^{2}+5\cdot uv+3\cdot v^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Using the given formula  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{u}(f,g)=a_{0}b_{2}-a_{1}b_{1}+a_{2}b_{0}
= (1)(3)-(6)(5)+(1)(2)=3-30+2=-25.
\]

\[
\boxed{-25.0000}
\]

calibration_attempts.text:
**Part (a)**  

In \(\mathbb P^{2}\) Bézout’s theorem states that two projective plane curves of degrees \(d_{1}\) and \(d_{2}\) intersect in exactly  

\[
d_{1}\,d_{2}
\]

points, counted with multiplicity, provided they have no common component.  
Here the degrees are  

\[
d_{1}=1\quad(\text{a line}),\qquad d_{2}=4\quad(\text{a smooth quartic}),
\]

so  

\[
1\cdot 4 = 4 .
\]

Because the intersection is transverse, each intersection multiplicity equals \(1\); the four points are distinct.  

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x\) be the answer from part (a); thus \(x=4\).  
We consider a smooth plane curve of degree \(x=4\) over the finite field \(\mathbb F_{7}\) (so \(q=7\)).  

A smooth plane curve is a one‑dimensional projective variety, i.e. its **dimension** \(d=1\).  
The Lang–Weil estimate for the number of \(\mathbb F_{q}\)-rational points on a smooth \(d\)-dimensional variety says  

\[
\#C(\mathbb F_{q}) = q^{d}+O\!\left(q^{d-\frac12}\right).
\]

The leading term is therefore  

\[
q^{d}=7^{1}=7 .
\]

\[
\boxed{7.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Set \(y\) equal to the answer from part (b); hence \(y=7\).  
The family of plane curves is given in \(\mathbb P^{2}\times\mathbb P^{1}\) by  

\[
F_{t}(x,y,z)=x^{2}+y^{2}-t^{\,y}z^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}-t^{7}z^{2}=0,
\]

where \(t\) is the coordinate on the base \(\mathbb P^{1}\).

For a fixed parameter \(t\) the fiber is the conic  

\[
C_{t}:\;x^{2}+y^{2}=t^{7}z^{2}.
\]

A point \([x:y:z]\) on \(C_{t}\) is singular iff all partial derivatives of the defining polynomial vanish:

\[
\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=2x,\qquad 
\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=2y,\qquad 
\frac{\partial F}{\partial z}=-2t^{7}z .
\]

Thus a singular point must satisfy  

\[
x=0,\; y=0,\; t^{7}z=0.
\]

* If \(t^{7}\neq 0\) (i.e. \(t\neq 0\) in the affine chart), the condition forces \(z=0\), which together with \(x=y=0\) gives the forbidden point \([0:0:0]\); hence no singularities.

* If \(t^{7}=0\) (i.e. \(t=0\)), the equations reduce to \(x=y=0\) with no restriction on \(z\). The point \([0:0:1]\) lies on the curve and makes it singular. Hence the fiber over \(t=0\) is singular.

To treat the point \(t=\infty\) on \(\mathbb P^{1}\), write homogeneous base coordinates \([u:v]\) with \(t=u/v\). Multiplying the equation by \(v^{7}\) yields  

\[
v^{7}x^{2}+v^{7}y^{2}-u^{7}z^{2}=0.
\]

At the point \([u:v]=[1:0]\) (i.e. \(t=\infty\)) we obtain \(-z^{2}=0\), i.e. the double line \(z=0\). This fiber is non‑reduced and therefore singular.

Consequently the morphism fails to be smooth precisely over the two points  

\[
t=0\quad\text{and}\quad t=\infty
\]

of the base \(\mathbb P^{1}\).  

\[
\boxed{2.0000}
\]

---

**Final compiled answers**

ANSWERS: {"a": "4.0000", "b": "7.0000", "c": "2.0000"}

**Part (a)**  

Bézout’s theorem states that two projective plane curves of degrees \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) intersect in exactly \(d_1d_2\) points, counted with multiplicity, provided they have no common component.  
Here \(d_1=1\) (a line) and \(d_2=4\) (a smooth quartic). Because the intersection is transverse, every intersection point has multiplicity 1.  

\[
1\cdot 4 = 4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4.0000}

parts.text: Let D be the smooth cubic curve in the projective plane defined by the homogeneous equation X^3 + Y^3 + Z^3 = 0. A line ℓ in the plane can be written in dual coordinates as aX + bY + cZ = 0 with (a:b:c) ∈ ℙ^2*. The dual curve D^∨ is a degree‑6 curve in the dual plane given (up to scaling) by the equation a^6 + b^6 + c^6 = 0. Determine the value of the parameter t for the line ℓ_t: X + Y + t Z = 0 that makes ℓ_t tangent to D. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the morphism f : ℂ → ℂ defined by f(t) = t^2 + x·t. The Jacobian determinant of f at a point t is the derivative f'(t) = 2t + x. Compute the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant at t = 1. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Let y = your answer to part (b). Consider the two homogeneous linear polynomials in variables u, v:

    f(u,v) = u + y·v,
    g(u,v) = u - v.

Compute the resultant of f and g with respect to the variable u, and give its numerical value. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

\]

The extension degree \([\,\mathbb C(X):\mathbb C(x)\,]\) equals the degree of the minimal polynomial of \(y\) over \(\mathbb C(x)\).  
The polynomial \(y^{3}-x(x-1)\) is irreducible in \(\mathbb C(x)[y]\) (it is not a perfect cube), and it has degree 3 in \(y\). Hence  

\[
\deg f=[\,\mathbb C(X):\mathbb C(x)\,]=3 .
\]

Geometrically, for a generic value \(x_{0}\in\mathbf P^{1}\) the fibre is defined by

From part (a) we have \(x=3\).

\[

Its Jacobian (the derivative) is  

\[

A finite étale cover \(h:Z\to\mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbb C}\) of degree \(y\) is, by definition, a finite morphism that is unramified everywhere. For any geometric point of the base, the fibre of an étale cover consists of exactly as many points as the degree of the cover.  

The additional hypothesis that the geometric monodromy group acts **transitively** on a geometric fibre guarantees that the fibre is a single orbit, but it does not change its cardinality. Therefore each geometric fibre contains precisely \(y\) points.

**Part (a)**  

On the affine chart \(v\neq 0\) set \(v=1\) and write \(t=u/v\).  
Then  

\[
f([t:1])=[t^{5}+t^{3}:1]=[t^{3}(t^{2}+1):1].
\]

For a generic point \([c:1]\in\mathbb{P}^{1}\) we must solve  

\[
t^{5}+t^{3}=c\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad t^{5}+t^{3}-c=0 .
\]

This is a polynomial of degree 5, so for a generic value of \(c\) it has exactly five solutions in an algebraic closure (counted with multiplicity). Hence  

\[
\deg f = 5 .
\]

\[
\boxed{5.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x=5\). The conic is  

\[
Q(X,Y,Z)=5X^{2}+YZ .
\]

Writing \(Q=[X\;Y\;Z]\;M\;[X\;Y\;Z]^{T}\) gives the symmetric matrix  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
5 & 0 & 0\\[2pt]
0 & 0 & \tfrac12\\[2pt]
0 & \tfrac12 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its determinant is  

\[
\det M = 5\det\begin{pmatrix}0&\tfrac12\\[2pt]\tfrac12&0\end{pmatrix}
      =5\bigl(0\cdot0-\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12\bigr)
      =5\left(-\frac14\right)=-\frac54=-1.25 .
\]

\[
\boxed{-1.2500}
\]
